32 The current in a circuit component is 2.00 µA.
How many electrons pass through the component each second?
A
1.25 × 1013
B
1.25 × 1016
C
1.25 × 1019
D
1.25 × 1025

hints: Notice the current is $2.00 \text{ } \mu\text{A}$, so first convert it to amperes to get the charge in coulombs passing each second.
Recall that current is rate of flow of charge, $I = Q/t$, and each electron carries magnitude $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$.
Divide the charge per second by $e$ to get the number per second, and check the power of ten carefully when dividing by $10^{-6}$ and $10^{-19}$.
walkthrough: Current is charge per unit time, $I = Q/t$. For $t = 1 \text{ s}$, the charge passing is $Q = It$.
Convert the current: $I = 2.00 \text{ } \mu\text{A} = 2.00 \times 10^{-6} \text{ A}$, so $Q = 2.00 \times 10^{-6} \text{ C}$ in one second.
Each electron contributes charge of magnitude $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, so number per second is $n = Q/e$.

A.explanation: Charge per second is $2.00 \times 10^{-6} \text{ C}$ and dividing by $1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ per electron gives $1.25 \times 10^{13}$ electrons per second.

B.explanation: This is 1000 times too large and comes from using $2.00 \text{ mA}$ instead of $2.00 \text{ } \mu\text{A}$ when dividing charge per second by the elementary charge.

C.explanation: This is $10^6$ times too large and comes from using $2.00 \text{ A}$ instead of $2.00 \times 10^{-6} \text{ A}$ for the charge flowing per second.

D.explanation: This is far too large and comes from mishandling powers of ten when converting microamperes and dividing by $1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$.
